title: Build the circuit, understand every wire
subtitle: A beginner’s path from circuit graphs to a battery-powered Pico servo controller.
scope: Designed for a software developer starting with no electronics background. Algebra and units are enough for the worked examples.
Lessons use the current auto-switch low-voltage topology. The actuator touches only the exterior paddle; no mains wiring or switch-box modification is included.
The examples are calculations and design reasoning, not measurements of your hardware. Manufacturer references are linked for each lesson.

sources.title: SparkFun: voltage, current, resistance and Ohm’s law
claims: Voltage is a difference between two points; current is charge flow per unit time; V = I R for an ohmic resistor.

sources.title: SparkFun: series and parallel circuits
claims: Series elements share current; parallel branches share end nodes; a node represents an electrical junction.

sources.title: SparkFun: electric power
claims: Electrical power P = V I; component power ratings limit heat dissipation.

sources.title: Raspberry Pi: Hardware design with RP2040, §3.1.1
claims: Explicitly covers Pico and Pico W: VBUS connects USB power to VSYS through a diode; VSYS feeds the onboard 3.3 V regulator.
An external supply can feed VSYS through a separate Schottky diode for concurrent USB device use; do not bridge the supplies.
Pico W physical pin mapping in the guide schematic: GP15=20, GP16=21, GP17=22, GP26=31, GND=38, VSYS=39, VBUS=40.

sources.title: Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W datasheet, §§2.1, 3.3–3.5
claims: VBUS nominally 5 V when USB is powered; VSYS allowed range 1.8–5.5 V; 3V3 is regulator output; I/O voltage fixed at 3.3 V.
Separate USB and external-source diodes provide power ORing into VSYS.
ADC and pin numbering requirements; board antenna and mounting features require clearances.

sources.title: SparkFun: diodes
claims: Diodes conduct predominantly in one direction, with forward voltage drop and reverse limits; Schottky diodes generally reduce forward loss.

sources.title: SparkFun: polarity
claims: Diode body band marks cathode; polarity markings must be interpreted for the specific component.

sources.title: Pololu S18V20F5 / item 2574
claims: Fixed 5 V step-up/step-down regulator; output current depends on input voltage and thermal conditions; typical efficiency 80–90%.
About 1 mA typical no-load current under many conditions. ENABLE is pulled toward protected VIN; leave unused ENABLE disconnected.
The disabled SEPIC regulator does not provide complete input/output isolation.

sources.title: Pololu Mini MOSFET Slide Switch LV / item 2810
claims: High-side MOSFET power path is controlled by the slider or ON input. With slider OFF, ON low/disconnected is off and above approximately 1 V is on.
Switching wiring inductance can create positive input and negative output transients; keep wiring short and use appropriate capacitors/clamps.
This switch is not an emergency disconnect; thermal current ratings depend on test conditions.

sources.title: Pololu: servo control interface in detail
claims: Servo command is encoded by positive pulse duration; typical period is 20 ms; angle mapping and endpoints are not standardized.
Servo electrical current varies with load and control behavior; signal timing does not replace the separate power connection.

sources.title: MicroPython machine.PWM reference
claims: PWM exposes frequency and duty/pulse-duration controls; hardware resources and behavior are port-dependent.

sources.title: SparkFun: voltage dividers
claims: For a lightly loaded divider, Vout = Vin Rbottom / (Rtop + Rbottom); a divider is unsuitable as a motor supply.

sources.title: MicroPython machine.ADC reference
claims: read_u16 returns a value scaled to 0–65535; scaling is not a promise of 16 bits of physical accuracy.

sources.title: SparkFun: capacitors
claims: Capacitors store electrical energy, resist abrupt voltage changes, have voltage limits and nonideal losses; some types require correct polarity.

sources.title: Panasonic eneloop lineup
claims: AA eneloop capacity varies by product generation; project estimator uses the cited 1900 mAh minimum family and 1.2 V nominal cells.
Discharge performance depends on conditions; nominal ratings are not measured project runtime.

sources.title: Panasonic eneloop FAQ
claims: Use matched cells together, insert correctly, and do not mix chemistry, capacity, age or charge state.
Primary dry cells must not be recharged; use the appropriate charger for the actual rechargeable chemistry.

sources.title: SCHURTER SPT 5×20 datasheet
claims: 0001.2507 is a 2 A time-lag fuse with AC/DC ratings and specified pre-arcing time/current behavior, not an instantaneous 2 A limiter.

sources.title: Adafruit: measuring voltage
claims: Voltage is measured between two points with voltage-mode probes in parallel with the subject.

sources.title: Adafruit: measuring current
claims: Current measurement inserts the meter in the current path and requires the correct input jack and range; placing a current-mode meter across a supply creates a short.

sources.title: Adafruit: multimeters overview and continuity
claims: Resistance and continuity checks require an unpowered circuit; continuity indicates low resistance, not necessarily a fault.

sources.title: Adafruit: making a good solder joint
claims: Heat both pad and conductor, feed solder to the joint, allow undisturbed cooling and trim wire leads.

sources.title: Adafruit quarter-size Perma-Proto / item 1608
claims: The prototype board has connected rows and rails; its holes are not all electrically isolated.

sources.title: auto-switch: power modes, assumptions and bench validation
claims: Project-specific source, not an independent authority: current Daily mode disables WLAN during ordinary waits; it does not establish deep sleep.
The 4.4 V software guard inhibits actuation and does not disconnect the full pack; runtime numbers are assumptions until measured.

sources.title: SparkFun: pull-up and pull-down resistors
claims: A pull resistor biases a node when it is not actively driven; an otherwise undefined node can float.
The resistor limits current when another driver establishes the opposing logic level; a direct connection would short that driver.
These are general concepts, not specifications for the reset state, input impedance or required resistor value of a particular Pico pin.

lessons.title: 1. Read a circuit as a graph
lessons.objective: Trace a complete supply-and-return path and recognize shared nets.
lessons.concept: A schematic describes connectivity, not the physical route of wires. A net is a named collection of connected terminals: much like one shared object referenced from several places. A junction dot joins lines; a crossing without a junction does not automatically join them. Series means one current path; parallel branches connect across the same pair of nodes. GND is our chosen zero-volt reference and return connection, not a place that consumes electricity or necessarily a connection to Earth.
lessons.project: Battery negative, Pico GND and servo GND share one net. The Pico and servo occupy separate power branches. Their wires meet at the power assembly so motor return current does not pass through the Pico board.

misconception.claim: Connecting only the positive wire should power the servo.
misconception.correction: The intended load circuit also needs a return path. The signal wire is not a substitute for a power return.

example.prompt: Find the loop when the servo gate is on.
steps: Start at battery positive, follow fuse → master → regulator → servo gate → servo power.
Return from servo GND to regulator/battery GND. The converter transfers energy between its input and output circuits.
example.answer: The ground wiring is part of the circuit, even when a diagram hides it behind repeated GND symbols.

quiz.question: Two distant points both labeled GND are…
options: The same electrical net in this design
Both connected to the wall’s earth wire
quiz.explanation: Net labels express connections; this battery circuit does not require a mains-earth connection.

quiz.question: Why route servo ground directly to the power assembly?
options: To keep its motor current out of the Pico return wiring
To give the servo a different zero volts
quiz.explanation: Common ground still exists; the physical route prevents motor current from sharing a sensitive board path.

lessons.title: 2. Voltage, current and resistance
lessons.objective: Use units correctly and distinguish a supply rating from actual current.
lessons.concept: Voltage (V) is a difference in electrical potential between two points. Current (A) is charge flowing per second. Resistance (Ω) relates voltage and current in an ohmic resistor: I = V/R. A 5 V supply rated for 2 A attempts to maintain 5 V while supplying the current the load demands within its capability; it does not force 2 A through every device. A motor and its controller are changing loads, not one fixed resistor.
lessons.project: We use 1 kΩ resistors in signal wires and one 1 kΩ resistor across the switched servo rail. The latter bleeds away stored charge after switch-off; the signal resistors limit some fault currents but do not convert 5 V logic into 3.3 V logic.

misconception.claim: A GPIO that reads 3.3 V can supply any load needing 3.3 V.
misconception.correction: Voltage compatibility and current capability are separate requirements. GPIO is intended for logic signaling.

example.prompt: How much current does the 1 kΩ bleeder draw from 5 V?
example.answer: 5 mA while the switched rail is at 5 V.

quiz.question: A 5 V load draws 0.3 A from a capable 5 V / 2 A supply. What flows?
options: 2 A because the label says so
quiz.explanation: The current rating is capacity; the load determines operating demand.

quiz.question: Doubling the voltage across the same ideal resistor does what?
quiz.explanation: I = V/R, with R unchanged. This exercise is about a resistor, not servo stall behavior.

lessons.title: 3. Power, batteries and response time
lessons.objective: Convert voltage and current to energy, then budget average use.
lessons.concept: Power is the rate of energy use: P = V × I in watts. Energy is power multiplied by time: watt-hours (Wh). A milliamp-hour rating measures charge, so compare different-voltage supplies in Wh. Four matched 1.2 V, 1900 mAh cells in series give about 4.8 V and 1900 mAh, or 9.12 Wh nominal. Series raises voltage; it does not quadruple Ah. Real usable energy is lower and condition-dependent.
lessons.project: Demo keeps the network responsive. Daily turns WLAN off between polls; the gateway holds commands meanwhile. Current firmware still waits awake rather than proving deep sleep. Include waiting, Wi-Fi reconnects, movement, regulator losses and indicator LEDs. A fast peak can reset a board even when total stored energy is ample.

misconception.claim: Sleeping five times longer must make battery life five times longer.
misconception.correction: Fixed waiting current and hardware overhead remain. Measure current over the full cycle, including failed reconnects.

example.prompt: Assume a 5 V branch draws 50 mA continuously. What does it use per day?
steps: E = 0.25 × 24 = 6 Wh per day before conversion losses.
For comparison, 20 hypothetical 5 V, 0.5 A, 1-second movements use 0.0139 Wh.
example.answer: In this assumed scenario, continuous electronics dominate; these are not measured Pico or servo currents.

quiz.question: Four series 1900 mAh cells have what nominal capacity?
quiz.explanation: Each cell carries the same current through the series chain. Nominal pack voltage is added.

quiz.question: A command arrives just after a Daily poll. What happens?
options: The Mac mini remotely wakes a powered-off radio instantly
The command waits for the next poll
quiz.explanation: Queueing trades command pickup time for reduced radio activity; current firmware does not provide an instant radio wake channel.

lessons.title: 4. How the Pico itself gets power
lessons.objective: Identify VBUS, VSYS, 3V3 and the difference between physical pins and GPIO numbers.
lessons.concept: VBUS, physical pin 40, is the USB connector’s power line: nominally 5 V when USB is powered. VSYS, physical pin 39, feeds the Pico’s onboard regulator, which produces 3.3 V for the chip, radio and GPIO circuitry. The USB line reaches VSYS through an onboard diode. 3V3, physical pin 36, exposes the regulated 3.3 V supply. The external VSYS operating range is 1.8–5.5 V, not arbitrary battery voltage.
lessons.project: Our battery → fuse → master → 5 V regulator → external diode D1 → VSYS path powers the Pico. GND returns through physical pin 38. Headerless solder pads have the same numbering as header pins. GP15 is physical pin 20; these are two naming systems for the same connection.

misconception.claim: Battery power on VSYS makes the VBUS pin output 5 V.
misconception.correction: The onboard diode blocks that reverse path; the Pico has no built-in 5 V boost output on VBUS.

example.prompt: USB is unplugged and external D1 delivers 4.7 V to VSYS. What powers the processor?
steps: The onboard regulator receives 4.7 V on VSYS.
It produces 3.3 V for board electronics.
VBUS remains normally unpowered.
example.answer: The Pico runs from VSYS even though there is no USB cable.

quiz.question: Which project connection actually supplies the Pico with battery energy?
options: D1 cathode to VSYS, physical pin 39
quiz.explanation: VSYS is the system power input; GPIO control wires do not power the board.

quiz.question: Where do you solder the gate-control wire for GP15?
quiz.explanation: Look up both labels on the official pinout before soldering. Headers change the connector style, not this mapping.

lessons.title: 5. Diodes and two power sources
lessons.objective: Explain why both USB and battery power can be connected without joining their supply outputs.
lessons.concept: A forward-biased diode conducts mainly from anode to cathode, with a voltage drop that depends on current and temperature. A reverse-biased diode largely blocks current within its ratings; it is not a perfect valve. A band on our axial diode marks the cathode. Two diodes can feed one node from separate sources: power ORing. The source with the higher delivered voltage tends to supply the load; close voltages may share. This is not a guaranteed priority selector or charger.
lessons.project: USB → onboard diode → VSYS and regulated battery 5 V → external D1 → VSYS meet only after their diodes. D1’s stripe faces VSYS. It prevents USB from feeding backward into the external 5 V/servo branch. Leave VBUS unwired externally; do not bridge VBUS to VSYS.

misconception.claim: The master switch being off guarantees the Pico is off.
misconception.correction: USB can still power the Pico. Disconnect USB and the battery connector for servicing.

example.prompt: With USB plugged in and the battery master off, can the servo move?
steps: USB feeds VSYS through the onboard diode.
External D1 blocks flow from VSYS back to the servo supply.
The servo branch has no battery power.
example.answer: The Pico can run, but USB alone does not power this design’s servo rail or recharge the cells.

quiz.question: Which way does D1’s stripe face?
quiz.explanation: The stripe is the cathode. Forward current enters the anode at external 5 V and exits toward VSYS.

quiz.question: Does our dual-source wiring guarantee USB is used first?
options: No: actual voltages and diode drops decide
quiz.explanation: Diode ORing operates electrically, without software selection.

lessons.title: 6. Turn a changing battery voltage into 5 V
lessons.objective: Choose a regulator using both voltage range and load demand.
lessons.concept: A buck converter lowers voltage; a boost converter raises it. A buck-boost function handles either side of the output target. Our selected 5 V S18V20F5 can do this as the four-cell pack changes voltage. Conversion is not free: input power exceeds output power, and available output current depends on input voltage and heat. A headline current rating is not a universal guarantee.
lessons.project: The regulator powers both branches continuously while the master is on. Its ENABLE pin is pulled toward battery VIN; leave it disconnected here rather than wiring it directly to a 3.3 V GPIO. It is a different interface from the servo gate’s ON input.

misconception.claim: A regulator providing 1 A at 5 V draws exactly 1 A from any battery.
misconception.correction: Power, not current alone, must balance. Lower input voltage may require more input current.

example.prompt: Estimate pack current for a hypothetical 5 V, 1 A load at 4.4 V and 85% efficiency.
steps: Output power = 5 × 1 = 5 W.
Input power ≈ 5/0.85 = 5.88 W.
Input current ≈ 5.88/4.4 = 1.34 A, plus separately modeled overhead.
example.answer: About 1.34 A under these assumptions; measure the actual circuit and do not treat this as a servo specification.

quiz.question: Why select a step-up/step-down regulator?
options: The pack can be above or below the desired 5 V
To convert every GPIO to 5 V
quiz.explanation: The output target is fixed while the input changes during discharge.

quiz.question: Can regulator ENABLE be copied onto the GP15 wire from the gate diagram?
options: Yes, all enable pins are identical
No, this ENABLE is pulled toward VIN
Only if a shorter wire is used
quiz.explanation: Read the exact module’s input circuit. Similar labels do not imply compatible electrical limits.

lessons.title: 7. Separate control from motor power
lessons.objective: Explain the separate motor-power path and why a resistor establishes an overridable default for its control input.
lessons.concept:
A MOSFET can act as an electronic switch: a small control signal changes a separate, larger-current path. Our assembled high-side switch interrupts the positive servo supply while preserving common ground. With its physical slider OFF, the selected module accepts a high ON input to conduct; low or disconnected means off. The Pico provides the instruction while the battery/regulator supplies the motor energy.

A pin that is high impedance is not actively forcing the connected wire HIGH or LOW. If nothing else establishes that wire’s voltage, it can float: leakage and electrical noise can affect its level. High impedance does not automatically mean floating; another component can define the voltage. Before software configures an output, or during reset, do not rely on your program to hold it LOW. Exact reset settings vary by chip and pin; this lesson does not assume a particular RP2040 or RP2350 reset level.
lessons.project:
GP15 → gate ON; a 100 kΩ pulldown connects that shared control node to GND. It provides a weak path toward LOW when the Pico is not actively driving it. This selected gate module already specifies OFF when ON is disconnected; our external pulldown also gives the wired control node an explicit low bias. A configured output can still drive HIGH against the resistor.

A direct ON-to-GND wire would hold the node at ground and short the GPIO output to ground when it tried to drive HIGH. The resistor instead limits that opposing current. GP15 supplies only the control-input current, pulldown current and brief charging current associated with changing the signal; it does not supply the servo’s motor current.

Keep the servo module’s physical slider OFF or it overrides software shutdown. After a completed movement, return the arm clear, stop pulses and drive the signal LOW, then set GP15 LOW. The servo rail decays while the independent D1 → VSYS branch keeps the Pico powered. The separate master switch controls the external battery branch.

misconception.claim: Setting the servo command to zero is the same as disconnecting its power.
misconception.correction: A control input and a power rail are different wires. Stopping commands alone does not guarantee zero servo consumption.

example.prompt: GP15 is driving 3.3 V. How much current flows through the 100 kΩ pulldown to GND?
steps: 0.000033 A = 33 µA = 0.033 mA. This is only the resistor’s current, not the entire gate module or servo current.
example.answer: 33 µA through the pulldown while the node is at 3.3 V. That small load allows the GPIO to establish HIGH; a direct wire to GND would not.

quiz.question: Where does servo motor current flow?
options: Through the gate’s VIN → VOUT path
quiz.explanation: The gate’s VIN → VOUT path carries motor current. GP15 only drives the control node and its small electrical loads, including the pulldown.

quiz.question: Why use a 100 kΩ pulldown instead of a direct ON-to-GND wire?
options: The resistor converts the motor’s 5 V into 3.3 V
It establishes a weak LOW default that GP15 can override with only 33 µA through the resistor at 3.3 V
A direct wire would make the GPIO stronger
quiz.explanation: A direct wire holds the node at GND and shorts a HIGH-driving output. The resistor provides a low default while allowing the GPIO to drive HIGH. The servo gate’s physical slider must still stay OFF.

lessons.title: 8. Send a position request to a servo
lessons.objective: Distinguish pulse duration, logic voltage, motor voltage and real position.
lessons.concept: A hobby servo has supply, ground and command wires. Position commands use the duration of repeating high pulses; around 20 ms between pulses is a common starting period. PWM hardware can generate them, but the meaningful command is pulse width, not simply duty percentage. A nominal 1.5 ms command is often called neutral; no universal mapping guarantees a particular angle or safe end stop.
lessons.project: GP16/GP17 produce command pulses through separate 1 kΩ resistors. Start with an unloaded servo, horn removed, and small calibrated pulse changes. Verify that the actual servo accepts 3.3 V logic. Its internal position loop does not report the room light’s state to the Pico.

misconception.claim: Calling an API “90 degrees” proves the shaft is at 90 degrees and the light is on.
misconception.correction: An API maps values to pulses. Mechanical calibration and a separate state sensor would be needed to establish actual switch/light state.

example.prompt: At 50 Hz, what is the period and duty fraction for a 1.5 ms pulse?
steps: Period = 1/50 s = 20 ms.
Duty fraction = 1.5/20 = 0.075.
example.answer: 7.5% at this frequency; changing frequency while keeping 7.5% duty changes the pulse duration.

quiz.question: You halve the period but keep 1.5 ms pulse width. Which command parameter stays the same?
quiz.explanation: Pulse width remains 1.5 ms while duty fraction doubles. Do not change period outside the actual servo’s limits.

quiz.question: What establishes usable movement endpoints?
options: Testing and calibrating the actual servo and mechanism
quiz.explanation: Servo mappings and mechanism interference vary. Avoid driving into a stop.

lessons.title: 9. Measure battery voltage with an ADC
lessons.objective: Design the divider and distinguish volts from state of charge.
lessons.concept: An analog-to-digital converter samples a voltage and represents it numerically. Our ADC pin must stay within the board’s allowed range. Two resistors scale pack voltage: Vadc = Vpack × Rbottom/(Rtop + Rbottom), assuming a lightly loaded divider. The return resistor is essential. read_u16 gives a scaled number, not 16 bits of measurement accuracy.
lessons.project: After the master: pack → 100 kΩ → GP26/ADC0 node → 47 kΩ → GND. A 100 nF capacitor also connects that node to GND. Sense the raw pack, since regulated 5 V hides discharge. Calibrate against a meter. A voltage percentage is approximate; the 4.4 V software guard stops new movement but does not disconnect all pack loads.

misconception.claim: Two resistors making 3.3 V can replace the power regulator.
misconception.correction: Loading the divider changes its output. It is for measurement here, not powering a servo.

example.prompt: What should this nominal divider output at a 4.8 V pack?
steps: Recover Vpack = Vadc × 147/47.
example.answer: About 1.535 V; component tolerance, ADC reference, noise and loading cause real error.

quiz.question: Why not infer remaining battery from the regulated 5 V rail?
options: It remains regulated across much of the discharge
The ADC can only read digital ones
quiz.explanation: Regulation deliberately hides changes in input voltage.

quiz.question: Is a pack voltage reading a complete battery protection system?
options: No: it cannot prove each cell’s condition or disconnect the load
quiz.explanation: A weak cell can be hidden in a total; our firmware guard is only an actuation inhibit.

lessons.title: 10. Handle short disturbances
lessons.objective: Explain capacitors, clamps and the difference between a transient and sustained overload.
lessons.concept: A capacitor stores energy and can briefly supply changing current. Capacitance is measured in farads: 470 µF = 0.000470 F. An ideal isolated capacitor obeys ΔV = I × Δt/C for constant discharge current. Real parts also have resistance, leakage and voltage limits. Wiring has inductance, so abruptly interrupting motor current can produce voltage excursions.
lessons.project: C1 is a 470 µF, 10 V electrolytic across unswitched 5 V and GND, close to the gate input; its negative stripe faces GND. D2 is a Schottky across the switched servo output, anode at GND and stripe at servo positive, to limit negative excursions. Neither guarantees clean waveforms without testing the finished wiring.

misconception.claim: Adding a large capacitor makes any weak supply adequate for a stalled servo.
misconception.correction: Stored energy is finite. Supply current, wiring and mechanical limits still matter.

example.prompt: If an isolated ideal 470 µF capacitor supplied 0.5 A for 1 ms, how far would its voltage fall?
steps: ΔV ≈ 1.06 V; ignore regulator support and capacitor losses for this exercise.
example.answer: About 1.06 V: even a visibly large capacitor is only a short-term buffer.

quiz.question: Why is D2 reverse-biased during normal 5 V operation?
options: It should short the supply normally
It should conduct only when the output goes sufficiently below GND
It is a second battery charger
quiz.explanation: Anode at GND and cathode at output form a negative-voltage clamp.

quiz.question: Where does C1’s negative stripe connect?
quiz.explanation: The selected electrolytic is polarized; polarity and voltage rating matter.

lessons.title: 11. Turn the graph into a physical assembly
lessons.objective: Choose protection and make connections that match the schematic.
lessons.concept: A fuse intentionally opens under specified overcurrent conditions. A time-lag fuse tolerates some brief current surges; its current label is not an instant electronic limit. Connector contacts, wire, solder joints and board traces must also carry the load. A bill of materials (BOM) names exact parts and quantities; a schematic names connections; an STL describes plastic geometry. None proves the others correct.
lessons.project: Place F1 close to battery positive, then the detachable keyed connector and master switch. Use matched removable NiMH cells and their proper external charger. The headerless Pico can use direct soldered leads and strain relief. Perma-Proto rows/rails are already connected: plan holes against the netlist before soldering. Heat pad and wire together, let solder wet both, cool without movement, then inspect and meter.

misconception.claim: If each purchased part fits its printed pocket, the assembly is verified.
misconception.correction: Also check solder joints, wire bends, plug insertion, service access, motion sweep, tolerances and electrical performance.

example.prompt: You find a spare prototype-board hole beside a signal wire. Can you attach ground there?
steps: Inspect the board’s copper pattern.
Use a continuity check with all power removed.
Confirm the hole belongs to the intended ground net rather than the signal’s connected row.
example.answer: Only after checking connectivity. A nearby hole is not necessarily a separate terminal.

quiz.question: Does a 2 A time-lag fuse prevent every current spike above 2 A?
options: No: opening depends on magnitude and duration
quiz.explanation: Use its time/current characteristic and test normal startup; it is not a current-regulated supply.

quiz.question: Which cell handling matches this design?
options: Charge mixed alkaline and NiMH together
Use matched NiMH cells, remove and charge with their proper charger
Solder directly to each cell for fewer contacts
quiz.explanation: The selected holder supplies contacts; maintain a matched set and correct polarity.

lessons.title: 12. Bring it up in stages
lessons.objective: Use a meter correctly and separate software, power and mechanical failures.
lessons.concept: A voltmeter probes between two points without becoming the main load path. A current meter goes in series with a load and has low resistance; putting it across battery positive and negative creates a short. Use the instrument’s specified jack, range and fuse, then return the red lead to its voltage jack after current work. Resistance/continuity tests use the meter’s own stimulus, so remove batteries and USB and verify discharged rails first.
lessons.project: Commission in stages: inspect unpowered wiring; measure regulator and divider with Pico/servo disconnected; power Pico and verify default gate-off; connect one unloaded servo; then test a supported mechanism. A basic meter can miss brief droop/spikes: a scope or suitable current logger may be needed. Record failures and measurements rather than increasing force blindly.

misconception.claim: A moving servo proves the entire design is ready for the wall.
misconception.correction: It proves one trial moved. Reboots, bad Wi-Fi, weak batteries, obstructions and repeated motion are separate cases.

example.prompt: The Pico resets when the servo starts. What should you investigate first?
steps: Remove mechanical load and test one servo.
Measure supply droop and inspect short, common power/ground routes.
Check startup current against the battery, regulator, fuse and wiring limits; inspect pulses separately.
example.answer: Treat a possible power transient as evidence to measure, not proof that the firmware needs a longer delay.

quiz.question: How do you measure the 5 V rail?
options: DC volts, probes between 5 V and GND
Current mode directly across 5 V and GND
quiz.explanation: Voltage is measured across two nodes; current mode across the supply can short it.

quiz.question: Before a continuity check, what must you do?
options: Disconnect batteries and USB, verify rails discharged
Leave USB connected for a ground reference
quiz.explanation: USB may power the Pico even with the master off. Use resistance/continuity only on an unpowered circuit.

capstone.title: Design auto-switch from a blank page
capstone.brief: Draw your own low-voltage circuit before revealing the expected decisions. Explain every wire using the lessons. This exercise checks reasoning; it does not certify an unbuilt circuit.

steps.title: 1. Write the requirements
steps.prompt: List the energy source, loads, control signals and measurements.
steps.expected: Four matched AA NiMH cells; a Pico W; one or two independently commanded servos with one moving at a time; common ground; manual master; switchable servo power; battery-voltage sensing; USB service access; Daily/Demo modes.

steps.title: 2. Draw the two power branches
steps.prompt: Start at the battery. How does the Pico stay alive with the servo off?
steps.expected: Battery positive → fuse → detachable connector → master → regulator VIN; regulator 5 V branches to D1 anode → cathode/stripe → Pico VSYS and separately to servo gate VIN → VOUT → servo power. Battery negative, modules, Pico and servo share GND. Pico includes its own VSYS → 3.3 V regulator.

steps.title: 3. Add USB without tying supplies together
steps.prompt: Trace USB energy and show the blocked reverse paths.
steps.expected: USB VBUS → onboard diode → VSYS. Our D1 also ends at VSYS. Leave external VBUS unconnected. Do not bridge VBUS/VSYS. USB can run the Pico with battery master off but cannot power this servo branch or charge the cells through VSYS.

steps.title: 4. Add signals and defaults
steps.prompt: Which physical pads, resistors and switch setting implement control?
steps.expected: GP15/pin20 → gate ON and 100 kΩ pulldown → GND; servo gate slider stays OFF. GP16/pin21 and optional GP17/pin22 → individual 1 kΩ resistors → servo signals. Motor power bypasses GPIO. Return signal low when power is removed; verify actual 3.3 V input compatibility.

steps.title: 5. Add sensing and transient parts
steps.prompt: Which nodes connect R_TOP, R_BOTTOM, C_ADC, C1 and D2?
steps.expected: Master-switched raw pack → 100 kΩ → ADC node/GP26/pin31 → 47 kΩ → GND; 100 nF across ADC node/GND. C1 positive at unswitched 5 V, negative at GND. D2 anode GND, cathode switched servo rail. A 1 kΩ bleeder spans switched servo rail/GND. Verify divider tolerance and physical wiring.

steps.title: 6. Budget and challenge the result
steps.prompt: What remains unproven after the diagram and CAD checks pass?
steps.expected: Measure pulse currents, rail droop, actual Wi-Fi waiting/reconnect energy, useful battery capacity, state-sensing limitations, physical fit, strain relief and motion forces. Compare rated limits at actual operating conditions. Hardware battery cutoff, exact servo dimensions and wall mounting remain distinct validation questions.

checklist: I can trace the Pico’s power and return path without using any signal wire.
I can explain why USB-only powers the Pico but not the servo in this circuit.
I distinguish GPIO names from physical pin numbers and use the correct board pinout.
I can calculate resistor current, power, divider voltage and nominal pack Wh with units.
I can explain every diode/capacitor polarity and why the power gate defaults off.
I can show how headerless solder wires, plugs and strain relief fit the mechanical model.
I know what the fuse, software cutoff and CAD checks do not establish.
I will verify unpowered connectivity, then measure one subsystem at a time before installing.

uncertainties: The user’s exact MG90S manufacturer, connector pinout, stall/current profile, pulse endpoints, spline and ear-hole geometry require checking.
Direct 3.3 V servo command compatibility must be checked on the actual servo; a series resistor is not a level shifter.
Board variant must match its MicroPython firmware. Headerless mounting removes header height, but soldered-wire clearance and service access remain real dimensions.
The power diagram is a reviewed prototype topology, not a fabricated and bench-validated PCB. Module thermal behavior and transient protection need tests.
NiMH state of charge and battery runtime are estimates until measured; the software low-voltage guard does not disconnect the full pack.
A nominal CAD clearance does not certify fit of real parts or mounting to a textured wall.
